uncertain.note: a raised comma-shaped sort stands between the full stop of 'ans.' and the T of 'Tant', at ascender height; transcribed as an apostrophe as printed. It makes no sense in the sentence and may be foul case.

uncertain.note: 'ni' and 'Ariſtote' are set almost touching; word division normalized per §1. The d of 'deuancier' at the line start is a filled ink blot; read as d from sense and the surviving ascender.

uncertain.text: en l'an quatorzieme, à l'hõme: & au douzieme, à là fem-
uncertain.note: the a of 'la' carries a heavy short stroke leaning like a grave, with spatter to its right (full/p003.jpg y~3260, x~1900, 6x; pages/strips/p003 last body strip, last line, 'à la fem-'). Thicker and blotchier than the grave of 'à' just before it; may be an accent sort or an ink blot. Transcribed as printed 'là' (sic; sense wants 'la'). Reader A read 'la'. | Carson-session 2026-09-21: mark ruled ink spatter; plain la

the final a is heavily inked and carries a short slanted stroke above it that could be read as a tilde ('lã'); 'Gloſe en la ſomme' is the sense, so it is read as a plain a with a stray mark. The line does end there — there is clear white space to its right.
the mark between 'xx' and 'q.' is set high and looks like a short dash rather than a point; read as the full stop the citation form requires (xx. q. i.).
a small dot sits between 'ſon' and 'diction'; much smaller than the note's commas and full stops, so taken as a speck. The word ends in a full n (the next line begins 'naire'), not a tilde.

the note's key letter is an italic k — a looped ascender plus a z-shaped leg — which at reading size looks like the two letters 'lz'. Read as key k, matching the {k} marker in the body. The first letter of 'Io.' is drawn with the same loop as the italic l, so the line could be read 'lo. And.'; 'Io. And. & Panor.' (Ioannes Andreae and Panormitanus) is the sense.
a small raised tick is printed between 'Panor.' and 'au'; transcribed as an apostrophe. It may be a broken sort or an offset mark.

the middle of the first word shows two strokes carrying what look like one or two dots, so it could be read 'diix.' or 'diux.'; 'dux.' (de eo qui duxit) is the reading taken. The ſ of 'cõſ.' is a long s.

the last letter has a closed bowl and reads as e, giving 'eſcriuane'; the sense wants 'eſcriuant' (S. Hierome eſcriuant ad Vitalem), so this may be a misprint or an inked-in italic t. Transcribed as read.
the letter before the stop is read as the æ ligature (à præ[lato]); at this size it could be a plain a.
the last letter before the stop has a tall crossed ascender: the italic t, not the short italic r. Read 'Paragt.' (sic for 'Paragr.'); reader A read 'Paragr.'
the mark after the swash italic D has a tail below the baseline and is read as a comma, unlike the plain round point after 'ea.' beside it; it could be a full stop.
the last line of note q ('& au vi. des' / 'loix.') is printed at the start of the foot block, before note r, because the margin ran out at the foot of the column; merged into note q as one note.
the gathering mark is printed 'A ij.' with a full stop after the j; kept as printed (p001 carries a bare 'A').

the margin is badly crowded on this page and every note after g starts well below its marker — h beside body line 9 (marker on line 6), l beside line 21 (marker on line 11), p beside line 36 (marker on line 24) — until note r is driven off the margin into the foot block. beside_line values were fixed by measuring the row positions of both columns (body pitch 45.2 px, margin pitch 36.5 px in pages/read/p003.jpg) and checked against the page image; the placements for m (line 25) and q (line 38) fall close to midway between two body lines.
